# Summary of Education in Sweden
Sweden’s education system is structured into several levels, starting from preschool (Förskola) offered to children aged 1 to 6, followed by a mandatory nine-year comprehensive school (Grundskola) covering ages roughly 7 to 16. The Grundskola is divided into stages: lower (grades 1–3), middle (grades 4–6), and upper (grades 7–9). Students study 16 compulsory subjects throughout Grundskola, including Swedish, English, mathematics, sciences, and social studies. Students receive grades starting from year 6, using a system from A to F (fail), with continuous assessment and national tests administered in grades 3, 6, and 9 to ensure standardization. In 2014, the National Agency for Education issued guidelines on handling instances of armed violence in schools due to a rise in reported threats and violence.
Post-compulsory education includes upper secondary school (Gymnasieskola), usually lasting three years (ages 16–19), divided into 18 national programmes split between preparatory and vocational tracks. Each programme comprises core courses and electives, culminating in a diploma project. Admission is based on compulsory grades from comprehensive school and is competitive. For students not meeting requirements, introductory programmes facilitate gaining eligibility for national programmes. Upper secondary education is highly accessible, with approximately 99% enrollment.
Higher education in Sweden follows the Bologna framework with bachelor’s (3 years), master’s (1–2 years), and doctoral levels (typically 4 years). Admission requires completion of upper secondary education or equivalent qualifications; postgraduate entry requires relevant prior degrees. Universities and university colleges offer academic and professional degrees, with grading systems varying but mostly criteria-referenced and compatible with European standards. The Swedish Scholastic Aptitude Test (SweSAT) provides alternative admission routes. Students benefit from governmental financial aid (CSN), though higher education is free only for Swedish, EU/EEA, and Swiss citizens.
Since the early 1990s, Sweden allows independent (free) schools (friskolor), which are publicly funded on a per-pupil basis and operate under non-discriminatory admission policies. These schools encompass varied pedagogical approaches (e.g., Montessori) and international or religious profiles but cannot charge fees. The free school system has grown significantly, reaching about 15% of upper secondary enrollment by 2023, sparking debate about equity, academic standards, and grading consistency. The Swedish system has influenced other countries, though opinions vary on its merits and challenges.
Sweden’s education system has shown fluctuating international assessment results; PISA tests between 2006 and 2012 revealed declines, though some improvements were noted in 2015. Factors such as immigration have been implicated in performance trends, although testing inconsistencies have also emerged. The government emphasizes inclusive education with special provisions for indigenous Sami schools and promotes adult education (Komvux) and vocational training. Violence in schools has risen, leading to official response guidelines to ensure safety and effective incident management.
